# How to write heartfelt birthday cards, wedding toasts and thank-you notes with Copilot

> **In short:** You can ask Microsoft Copilot to draft a birthday card, wedding toast or thank-you note from a few details about the person and the moment, then rewrite the draft in your own voice. Copilot gives you a starting point so you are not staring at a blank page — but it cannot know the person for you, so your edits are what make the message feel real.

Anyone can freeze up when a card or toast is due. The right words hide somewhere between your feelings and the page, and the clock is ticking. Microsoft Copilot is an AI assistant that lives in your browser, your phone, and inside apps like Word and Outlook. You give it a short description of who the message is for and what you want to say, and it writes a first draft in seconds. Your job is to read it, keep the parts that sound like you, and cut the parts that do not. The result is a message that feels personal without taking all evening to write.

## Before you start
- A free Microsoft account (the same one you use for Outlook, OneDrive, or Xbox). If you do not have one, you can create one in a couple of minutes at the official Microsoft sign-in page.
- A way to reach Copilot: a web browser on a computer, the Copilot app on your phone, or Microsoft Word with Copilot enabled. Any of these works.
- A few honest details about the person you are writing to — their name, what you appreciate about them, a memory you share, the tone you want (warm, funny, formal, brief).
- About 10 to 15 minutes for the whole thing: 2 minutes to set up, 3 to 5 minutes to prompt and edit, and a few more to copy the final version into your card or print it out.

## Step 1 — Open Copilot and start a new chat

In a browser, go to the official Copilot website and sign in with your Microsoft account. On a phone, open the Copilot app and tap the sign-in button. If you are in Microsoft Word, look for the **Copilot** option in the top ribbon. Once you are signed in, you land on a clean screen with a large text box near the bottom — that is the prompt box, the place where you type what you want. A new chat starts every time you load the page, so old messages will not confuse your new request. If you have used Copilot before and want a clean start, look for a button like a **new chat** or **pencil icon** at the top of the list of past conversations.

💬 Example: type `Help me write a birthday card for my sister.`

You'll know it worked when the screen shows your words in the prompt box and Copilot is ready to respond.

## Step 2 — Tell Copilot who the message is for and what you want to say

Click inside the prompt box and type a short description. A prompt is just the instruction you give to an AI. The more specific you are about the person and your feelings, the warmer the draft will be. Mention the recipient's name, your relationship, one thing you genuinely appreciate about them, and the tone you want. You do not need to write a lot — three or four sentences is plenty. If you are writing a wedding toast, also mention how long the toast should run when spoken out loud, usually one to two minutes. If you are writing a thank-you note, mention the specific gift or favor you are thankful for, because generic thanks can feel hollow.

💬 Example: `Write a warm birthday card for my dad, who is turning 70. He's a quiet, kind man who taught me to fish and always fixes things around the house. I want it to feel grateful and a little funny, not too long. About 80 words.`

You'll know it worked when Copilot replies with a short block of text that sounds like a real card — a greeting, a personal line, and a closing.

## Step 3 — Ask for a second version if the first one is not quite right

Read the draft out loud. If it sounds stiff, too formal, or just not like you, do not start over. Type a short follow-up asking for a change. Saying "make it warmer", "sound more like me talking to a close friend", or "add a small joke about our fishing trips" tells Copilot exactly how to adjust. This back-and-forth is normal — even short messages often need a second pass. Keep your edits as instructions, not as the full rewrite, so the AI does the heavy lifting and you stay in control of the feeling. If you would like a few options side by side, ask for two or three versions in the same message and pick the one you like best.

💬 Example: `That is good, but can you make it sound less formal? Add a line about the time he fell asleep in his fishing chair and the fish got away. Keep it under 100 words.`

You'll know it worked when the new draft has at least one line that genuinely sounds like something you would actually say.

## Step 4 — Add one true detail the AI cannot know

This is the step that turns a generic draft into a personal message. Think of one small true thing about the person or your relationship that you did not put in the prompt — a shared joke, a recent moment, a small habit you love. Type that detail into the chat and ask Copilot to weave it in. It might be the way your dad hums while he works, the inside joke from your sister's wedding, or the specific way a friend helped you last month. The AI cannot invent this on its own, which is exactly why your input is the most important part of the process. Once the detail is in, the message stops sounding like it could be for anyone and starts sounding like it is for one person.

💬 Example: `Can you add a line about how he still hums the same tune from the radio while he works in the garage? It's something I will always remember.`

You'll know it worked when the draft contains the small true detail in a way that feels natural, not forced.

## Step 5 — Edit the draft into your own voice

Read the latest version one more time and put on your editing hat. Cross out any phrase that does not sound like you, even if it is well written. Swap big words for small ones. Shorten sentences that run too long. Add a word you actually use, like "honestly" or "you know". If you are writing a toast, read it out loud once — your ear will catch anything that sounds like a press release instead of a real person talking. Copilot is your first-draft helper, not your ghostwriter, so the final version should pass the "would I actually say this?" test. A good rule of thumb is that at least half the words should feel familiar to you.

💬 Example: change *"I am eternally grateful for your unwavering guidance"* to *"Thanks for always being there, Dad. I notice it more every year."*

You'll know it worked when you can read the whole message without cringing at any single line.

## Step 6 — Copy the final version into your card, email or printout

Once the message sounds right, click the **copy** button that usually appears under Copilot's reply, or highlight the text and copy it yourself. Paste it into your card, your email, or a Word document you want to print. If the handwriting on the card matters to you, write the message by hand onto the card, using the draft as your script. If you used the Copilot add-on inside Word, the text is already in your document, so you can format and print straight away. For toasts, practice reading it once or twice before the event so the words feel natural in your mouth, not just on the page.

💬 Example: paste the draft into a blank card, print it on nice paper, or copy it into the notes app on your phone for the big day.

You'll know it worked when the message is sitting where it needs to be and you feel ready to send, write, or raise a glass.

## Common mistakes
- **Forgetting to add a real detail.** A clean draft with no personal touch reads like a greeting card from a store. Fix: always add at least one small true thing only you would know, even if it is just a phrase you and the recipient share.
- **Sending the AI's first draft untouched.** The first reply is rarely the best one. Fix: treat it like a rough sketch and spend two minutes editing so it sounds like you, not like a polite robot.
- **Asking for a toast that is way too long.** A two-minute spoken toast is about 200 to 250 words, shorter than most people think. Fix: tell Copilot the time limit and ask for a version that fits, then read it out loud to check the pace.
- **Using the wrong tone for the moment.** A formal thank-you note to your boss and a funny birthday card for your best friend need very different voices. Fix: name the tone you want in the prompt, and if the draft misses, say so and ask for a rewrite.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** The next time a birthday, wedding, baby shower, or thank-you slips up on you, you can go from blank page to a draft in under five minutes, and finish the personal part in another five. That is roughly a ten-minute job instead of an evening of dread.
- **For your business or work:** The same prompt-and-edit habit works for client thank-you notes, retirement messages for a colleague, or a short team toast at a work event. You bring the real detail about the person, Copilot helps you shape the words.
- **If you are just getting started:** Pick the next card or note you actually need to write this week. Open Copilot, paste the example prompt from Step 2 with your own details swapped in, and treat the reply as a starting point, not a final answer.

## Try it now
Open Copilot on your phone or computer, and write a real birthday card for someone whose birthday is coming up in the next month. Use the Step 2 example as your template, swap in one true memory of your own, and spend two minutes editing the draft until it sounds like you. Send the card, and notice how much lighter a small task feels when you do not have to start from zero.
